Another particle has a velocity function given by ${v}_{2}(t)=t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}).$ Evaluate the velocity of this particle at $t=\frac{16\pi }{3}.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${v}_{2}(\frac{16\pi }{3})\,=\,$

                                        $\text{m/s}$
feedback.worked_solution:
Evaluating the function ${v}_{2}(t)$ at $t=\frac{16\pi }{3}$, we get

$$
{v}_{2}(\frac{16\pi }{3})=(\frac{16\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{8\pi }{3})
$$

First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\frac{8\pi }{3}$ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8\pi }{3}-2\pi  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{8\pi }{3})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}).$

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13942110/assets/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{2\pi }{3}$ corresponds to the point $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{8\pi }{3})=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Finally, 

$$
{v}_{2}(\frac{16\pi }{3})=(\frac{16\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{8\pi }{3})=-\frac{8\pi }{3}.
$$
